items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The term 'Mouseketeer' refers to Steve Gadd, whom the interviewee discusses as a contemporary musician he has heard play and collaborated with on a video, but 'Mouseketeer' itself is not a person to judge a relationship with.

ctx.x: Shelly was a very – played with a lot of taste. He was never a so-called big-band drummer. He could do it, but he favored playing in small groups. Great with brushes. With the sticks he had a nice touch. Never got in the way. Musical. He was a musical player. Steve Gadd was – I just heard him play last week. That young man can do anything. He can play in any groove. He goes on the road with James Taylor, and it’s a certain way of playing. Got his own group, Gadd Gang. Plays in it, bebop style. He can play with…
As we were discussing yesterday, he also was a tap-dancer. You talked about being a Mouseketeer.

Right. He was a Mouseketeer. He doesn’t want to be reminded of that, but he was. Mickey Mouse and him are a distance away, but he was a Mouseketeer. There’s a video out called Time Grooves that Harold Farberman put out. The drummers are Steve Gadd, Alex Acuña, Harvey Mason, Vic Firth playing tympani, and David Friedman playing xylophone, and myself. Steve and I do a time-step, and I do a sand on that Time Grooves. Did you know about that one?

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Well a lot of the young drummers... Steve Gadd... are composing and writing... I’ve always wanted to do this, it’s a salute honoring twelve great drummers... Steve Gadd are the new guys

ctx.x: Oh — a drummer knows that, yes.

Well a lot of the young drummers, well some of the older guys like Tiny Kahn was a great orchestrator, great arranger. And today, Billy Cobham, Steve Gadd, Tony Williams, a lot of these guys are composing and writing, and Harvey Mason, drummers like that you know, not only great percussion players but they’re very sensitive as to what the music is all about.
And when was it that you really felt that you could become a professional musician?

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Steve Gadd plays all those rhythms now. He got them from studying the rudiments and studying some of those drummers.

ctx.x: The biography in The New Grove Dictionary of Jazz lists that you learned tap- dancing, or were a tap-dancer with a barrelhouse pianist, Speckled Red. You said that you played with him. Did you also – is that an accurate account? Were you also a tap dancer?

All the drummers during that era – Jo Jones, for example, Buddy Rich – Steve Gadd was a Mouseketeer. They all tap-danced. They told jokes. Because when you played the theaters, you did everything. You were m.c. You had a dance routine. You had a dance routine called a b.s. chorus. It was nothing but a series of taps. That’s how Baby Lawrence, Teddy Hale, Bunny Briggs – that’s where all those guys came up, from the tap-dance era. My sister Mary – full sister – taught me how to tap-dance. She taught me the…
How old were you when she was teaching you this?
